title: Desktop UI with Avalonia
text:
Introduction
This book collects the Desktop UI chapters of POSE in 5BHIF at HTL Leonding, school year 2026/27. You learn to build desktop applications with Avalonia and C#: from your first window to data binding and the MVVM pattern.
The book is meant to be worked through, not just read. Every chapter contains labs, highlighted in boxes like this one:
The labs of a chapter build on each other, so do them in order and keep your project between them.

title: Desktop UI with Avalonia
text:
Tools you need

the .NET 10 SDK
JetBrains Rider with the AvaloniaRider plugin, or Visual Studio Code with the Avalonia extension
Git and a GitHub account

title: 1  Avalonia Basics
text:
1.1 Why Avalonia?
Avalonia is a cross-platform UI framework for .NET. You describe the user interface in XAML, an XML-based markup language, and write the logic in C#. The same app runs on Windows, macOS and Linux, and Avalonia can also target the browser and mobile devices.
This chapter covers the foundations: how an Avalonia project is put together, how XAML works, and how a window reacts to clicks. Along the way you build your first app, HelloAvalonia, in four labs. Each lab starts from where the previous one stopped, so work through them in order.

title: 1  Avalonia Basics
text:
1.1.1 The landscape in 2026
There is no reliable market-share figure for desktop UI frameworks. Most desktop applications are internal tools that never show up in any statistic. The signals that do exist all point the same way:

Web frameworks such as React, Angular and Node.js are used by far more developers than any native desktop toolkit. Many “desktop” apps are web technology too: VS Code, Slack, Teams and Discord are built with Electron.
WPF, Microsoft’s Windows-only desktop framework, has the largest installed base in the .NET world. It is in maintenance mode, but countless enterprise, industrial, medical and finance applications run on it and still have to be maintained and extended.
Avalonia is the fastest-growing .NET desktop framework and the leading cross-platform one. Avalonia 12 was released in April 2026; JetBrains, Unity, Autodesk and NASA are among its users.

As a rough order: web and Electron apps are far ahead, then WPF and WinForms (both legacy), then Avalonia (growing), about level with MAUI and Qt.


1.1.2 Why learn it after three years of web development?

A different programming model. A desktop app is one long-running process that keeps its state, has a UI thread and binds the UI to data. A web app mostly answers stateless requests and re-renders a DOM. Desktop development makes you think about state and threading in ways web development rarely does.
WPF comes almost for free. Avalonia’s XAML, bindings, styles and the MVVM pattern map almost one to one onto WPF. Maintaining existing WPF code is where many junior .NET jobs are: machine control panels, test benches, in-house tools.
It runs everywhere, including on your own laptop, whatever operating system it has.
Some software doesn’t belong in a browser: anything that talks to hardware (serial ports, USB, fieldbuses), runs offline or in isolated networks, computes heavily on the local machine, or drives an embedded Linux touch panel.
Same stack as the backend. It is the same C#, the same tooling, the same dependency injection and the same unit tests you already know from ASP.NET Core.
The patterns transfer. Observable state, commands and composing a UI from components are close relatives of what React and Angular do.

To be honest about it: most of you will build more web frontends than desktop UIs. Avalonia widens your skill set; it doesn’t replace your web skills.

title: 1  Avalonia Basics
text:
1.2 Setting up
You need:

the .NET 10 SDK,
an IDE: JetBrains Rider with the AvaloniaRider plugin, or Visual Studio Code with the Avalonia for VS Code extension,
the Avalonia project templates. Install them once per machine:
dotnet new install Avalonia.Templates







TipLab 1.1: Create and run the project



🎯 Goal. An empty Avalonia app that starts and shows a window.

Create the project and a solution file for it:
dotnet new avalonia.app -n HelloAvalonia -o HelloAvalonia
cd HelloAvalonia
dotnet new sln -n HelloAvalonia
dotnet sln add HelloAvalonia.csproj
The solution file (HelloAvalonia.slnx) is optional for a single project, but it lets Rider open the folder as a solution.
Open HelloAvalonia.csproj and add one line to the first <PropertyGroup>:
<TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
From now on every compiler warning stops the build. Warnings are almost always real problems (a possible null, an unused variable), and this way you can’t ignore them.
Start the app:
dotnet run

✅ Check. A window titled HelloAvalonia opens and shows the text Welcome to Avalonia!. Close it before you continue.

title: 1  Avalonia Basics
1  Avalonia Basics
text:
1.4 XAML basics
XAML uses XML syntax, so the usual XML rules apply:

A file has exactly one root element, and all other elements are correctly nested inside it. For a window, the root is <Window>; for a reusable part of a UI, it is a <UserControl>.
Element and attribute names are case-sensitive, and attribute values are always in double quotes.
The nesting of elements forms a tree. Avalonia turns that tree into the UI.

Every element stands for a class. When the window is created, <Button> creates a Button object through its parameterless constructor. Every attribute sets a public property of that object or subscribes to one of its events:
<Button Background="AliceBlue" Content="Click me!"/>
The attribute values are strings. Behind the scenes, type converters turn them into the right type, for example "AliceBlue" into a brush.

1.4.1 Namespaces
The root element of every XAML file declares at least two XML namespaces:
xmlns="https://github.com/avaloniaui"
xmlns:x="http://schemas.microsoft.com/winfx/2006/xaml"

The first is the default namespace (no prefix). It contains all Avalonia controls, so you can write <Button> directly.
The second maps the XAML language namespace to the prefix x. Language features such as x:Class and x:Name come from there.

To use your own classes in XAML, declare a namespace for them with a prefix of your choice:
xmlns:models="using:HelloAvalonia.Models"
Then <models:Person/> creates a HelloAvalonia.Models.Person. For a class in a different assembly (another project or a NuGet package), the older form names the assembly as well: xmlns:logic="clr-namespace:LogicNamespace;assembly=Logic".


1.4.2 Property element syntax
Some values are too complex for a string. Instead of an attribute, you can then write the property as a child element named <Type.Property>:
<Button Background="AliceBlue">
    <Button.Content>
        <Ellipse Width="120" Height="90" Fill="LightBlue"/>
    </Button.Content>
</Button>
Here the button’s Content is no longer text but an Ellipse. Content is also the button’s content property, so you may leave out <Button.Content> and put the Ellipse directly between <Button> and </Button>.


1.4.3 Naming elements
To access an element from code, give it a name:
<TextBlock Name="CounterText" Text="Counter: 0"/>
The generated half of the partial class then contains a field CounterText of type TextBlock: the exact object the XAML created. x:Name="CounterText" does the same. Name is a property of the Avalonia controls, while x:Name is a XAML language feature that works on any element. For controls, use Name.


1.4.4 Markup extensions
Sometimes a property should not get a fixed value but one that comes from somewhere else. That is the job of markup extensions, written in curly braces. Here, the second button takes its background from the first:
<Button Name="Btn1" Background="LightYellow"/>
<Button Background="{Binding #Btn1.Background}"/>
#Btn1 refers to the element named Btn1. The most important markup extensions are:







Extension
Description




Binding
Takes the value from a data source and keeps it up to date (chapter Data Binding).


StaticResource
Takes the value from a resource, once, when the element is created.


DynamicResource
Takes the value from a resource and follows it when the resource changes.


TemplateBinding
Used inside a control template (chapter Styles).





1.4.5 Styled properties
Avalonia controls don’t use plain C# properties for most of their settings. They use styled properties, which are registered with Avalonia’s property system (AvaloniaProperty.Register). You set and read them like any other property, but they can do more:

they have default values,
they notify Avalonia whenever their value changes,
they can validate new values and run a callback when the value changes.

That is what makes data binding, styles and animations possible: all three only work with styled properties. Every property of a built-in control that you would want to style or bind already is one.


1.4.6 Attached properties
An attached property is set on one element but belongs to another, usually the layout container around it. In this example, each button says at which edge of the DockPanel it wants to be docked:
<DockPanel>
    <Button DockPanel.Dock="Top">Click me!</Button>
    <Button DockPanel.Dock="Bottom">Click me too!</Button>
</DockPanel>
DockPanel.Dock only makes sense on a child of a DockPanel. Without attached properties, Button would need a Dock property, plus a property for every other container it could ever be placed in. The same mechanism places elements in the rows and columns of a grid, as you’ll see next.

title: 1  Avalonia Basics
text:
1.5 A first layout
A Window can only have one direct child. To show more than one element, that child is a layout container (a panel), and everything else goes inside it. The two most common panels are:

Grid divides the space into rows and columns. RowDefinitions="*,Auto" creates two rows: the second is exactly as tall as its content (Auto), and the first takes all the remaining space (*). Children choose their row with the attached property Grid.Row.
StackPanel arranges its children one after another, vertically by default or horizontally with Orientation="Horizontal". Spacing adds a gap between the children.

The chapter Layouts and Controls covers all panels in detail.






TipLab 1.2: The layout



🎯 Goal. The window shows a greeting, a counter and four buttons. The buttons don’t do anything yet.
All changes are in MainWindow.axaml.

In the <Window> start tag, change the title to Title="Hello Avalonia" and add after it:
Width="480" Height="360" MinWidth="420" MinHeight="320"
WindowStartupLocation="CenterScreen"
Also set d:DesignWidth="480" and d:DesignHeight="360". The d: attributes only apply to the previewer in the IDE; mc:Ignorable="d" tells the compiler to skip them.
Replace the text Welcome to Avalonia! with a grid of two rows:
<Grid RowDefinitions="*,Auto" Margin="32">
</Grid>
Inside the grid, add the upper row, a StackPanel with the greeting:
<StackPanel Grid.Row="0" Spacing="20"
            VerticalAlignment="Center" HorizontalAlignment="Center">
    <TextBlock Text="Hello, Avalonia!" FontSize="36" FontWeight="SemiBold"
               HorizontalAlignment="Center"/>
</StackPanel>
In that StackPanel, below the greeting, add a button and the counter:
<Button Content="Click me!" Classes="accent" Padding="24,10"
        HorizontalAlignment="Center"/>
<TextBlock Text="Counter: 0" FontSize="16" Opacity="0.7"
           HorizontalAlignment="Center"/>
Classes="accent" paints the button in the system’s accent color (chapter Styles).
Below that StackPanel, still inside the grid, add the lower row:
<StackPanel Grid.Row="1" Orientation="Horizontal" Spacing="12"
            HorizontalAlignment="Center">
    <Button Content="Increment counter" Padding="16,8"/>
</StackPanel>
Then add two more buttons to it yourself: Popup message and Close, with the same padding.

✅ Check. dotnet run: the window is centered on the screen, the greeting and counter sit in the middle, and the three buttons are lined up along the bottom. Make the window narrower and wider: the layout adapts, but the window can’t get smaller than 420 × 320.

title: 1  Avalonia Basics
1  Avalonia Basics
1  Avalonia Basics
text:
1.8 Window events
Besides the events of its controls, a window has events of its own. The most useful ones:







Event
Occurs when




Opened
the window has been shown for the first time.


Loaded
the window and all its controls are created and laid out. Initialization code that needs the controls belongs here.


Activated / Deactivated
the window becomes the active window, or another window does.


PositionChanged
the window was moved.


SizeChanged
the window’s size changed.


Closing
the window is about to close. Setting e.Cancel = true in the handler keeps it open, e.g. to ask about unsaved changes.


Closed
the window has been closed.



There is no event for minimizing or maximizing. The WindowState property holds that state; subscribe to PropertyChanged and check whether e.Property is Window.WindowStateProperty to be notified.

title: 1  Avalonia Basics
text:
1.9 The previewer
Rider (with the AvaloniaRider plugin) and VS Code (with the Avalonia extension) render a live preview of an .axaml file next to the editor, without starting the app. That’s handy for adjusting a layout. The d: attributes from Lab 1.2 set the size of that preview.
The previewer is not completely reliable. It can lag behind your edits, keep showing an error you already fixed, or fail to load for reasons that have nothing to do with your XAML. A rebuild usually clears it. A red previewer is no proof that your XAML is wrong: check with dotnet build first.

title: 1  Avalonia Basics
text:
1.10 Try it yourself
Extend HelloAvalonia:

Add a button that resets the counter to 0.
Disable Increment counter once the counter reaches 10. Every control has an IsEnabled property.
Swap ShowAsync and ShowAsPopupAsync in the two dialog handlers and compare.
Add a TextBox and change the greeting dialog to greet the name entered there. A TextBox has a Text property.
Handle the window’s Closing event: ask “Do you really want to quit?” and keep the window open when the answer is No. Watch out: the handler can’t wait for the dialog before deciding, because the window closes as soon as the handler returns. Cancel first, ask, and call Close() yourself on Yes. Then make sure that this second Close() doesn’t ask again.

title: 2  Layouts and Controls
text:
2.1 Layout basics
A window can hold only one child. Everything else is arranged by panels: containers that decide where their children go and how big they are. This chapter introduces the panels you will use all the time, plus a few helpers around them.
In the labs you build LayoutDemo: a launcher window with one button per panel, each opening a small window where you try that panel out.
Every control also has a few properties that tell its panel how to place it:

title: 2  Layouts and Controls
text:
Panels (classes derived from Panel) hold any number of children. All other controls hold at most one child, usually in their Content property.
Panels can be nested: a Grid cell can contain a StackPanel, which contains another Grid, and so on. Real layouts are almost always nested.
Avoid fixed sizes. Let the panels size the controls, so the layout adapts when the window is resized or the text changes.
Layout runs in two passes: in the measure pass every element reports how much space it would like; in the arrange pass the panel assigns each child its final position and size.









Property
Meaning




HorizontalAlignment, VerticalAlignment
Stretch (fill the available space), Left/Top, Center, Right/Bottom


Margin
Space around the control: "10" on all sides, "10,5" left/right and top/bottom, "10,5,10,0" left, top, right, bottom


Padding
Space inside the control, between its border and its content


Width, Height, MinWidth, MaxWidth, …
Fixed or limited sizes; use sparingly









TipLab 2.1: The launcher



🎯 Goal. A launcher window with a Grid button that opens a second window.

Create the project as in Lab 1.1, but named LayoutDemo, including the solution file and TreatWarningsAsErrors.
In MainWindow.axaml, set Title="Layout Demo" Width="360" Height="560" and replace the text Welcome to Avalonia! with:
<StackPanel Margin="24" Spacing="10">
    <TextBlock Text="Layouts and Controls" FontSize="22" FontWeight="SemiBold"/>
    <Button Content="Grid" HorizontalAlignment="Stretch" Click="OnOpenGridClicked"/>
</StackPanel>
Create a second window. In the project folder, run:
dotnet new avalonia.window -n GridWindow
This creates GridWindow.axaml and GridWindow.axaml.cs. In GridWindow.axaml, set Title="Grid" Width="620" Height="560".
In MainWindow.axaml.cs, add using Avalonia.Interactivity; and this handler:
private void OnOpenGridClicked(object? sender, RoutedEventArgs e) => new GridWindow().Show();
Show() opens the window next to the launcher; you can open it several times. (Its sibling ShowDialog(this) would block the launcher until the new window is closed.)

✅ Check. The launcher shows a heading and a full-width Grid button. Each click opens a window Grid with the text Welcome to Avalonia!.
All further labs of this chapter follow the same pattern: create a window with dotnet new avalonia.window, give it a title and a size, and add a launcher button with a handler.

title: 2  Layouts and Controls
2  Layouts and Controls
2  Layouts and Controls
text:
2.4 DockPanel
A DockPanel attaches each child to one of its edges with the attached property DockPanel.Dock (Top, Bottom, Left, Right). The order matters: each child is docked into the space the previous children left over. With LastChildFill="True" (the default), the last child fills whatever remains.
In the direction it is docked, a child only gets the size it asks for. A button docked to the top is therefore only as tall as its text, even with VerticalAlignment="Stretch"; give it a Height to make it taller (a Width for Left/Right). Along the edge, Stretch fills the full length.






TipLab 2.5: DockPanel



🎯 Goal. Five buttons docked to different edges.

Create DockPanelWindow (title DockPanel, 420 × 320) and its launcher button.
Replace the window’s text with a DockPanel and its first two buttons:
<DockPanel Margin="16">
    <Button DockPanel.Dock="Top" Background="LightBlue" Height="50"
            HorizontalAlignment="Stretch"
            HorizontalContentAlignment="Center" VerticalContentAlignment="Center">Button1</Button>
    <Button DockPanel.Dock="Left" Background="LightGreen" Width="90"
            VerticalAlignment="Stretch"
            HorizontalContentAlignment="Center" VerticalContentAlignment="Center">Button2</Button>
</DockPanel>
HorizontalContentAlignment/VerticalContentAlignment center the text inside the larger button.
Add three more buttons yourself:

Button3, docked Right, LightCoral, 90 wide,
Button4, docked Top, LightYellow, 50 tall,
Button 5, not docked, LightGray, stretched in both directions.


✅ Check. Button1 spans the full width at the top. Button4 is also at the top, but only between Button2 and Button3, because it came later. Button 5 fills the middle.

💡 Try it. Move Button1 below Button2 in the XAML. Then set LastChildFill="False".

title: 2  Layouts and Controls
text:
2.5 WrapPanel
A WrapPanel works like a horizontal StackPanel, but starts a new line when the next child doesn’t fit any more. A StackPanel would simply let it run off the edge. With Orientation="Vertical" it fills columns instead of lines.






TipLab 2.6: WrapPanel



🎯 Goal. Nine buttons that wrap when the window gets narrow.

Create WrapPanelWindow (title WrapPanel, 380 × 360) and its launcher button.
Replace the window’s text with a <WrapPanel Margin="16"> containing nine buttons, Button1 to Button9.

✅ Check. The buttons fill a line, then continue on the next one. Make the window narrower and wider: the lines re-flow.

💡 Try it. Set Orientation="Vertical" and resize the window again.

title: 2  Layouts and Controls
2  Layouts and Controls
text:
2.7 UniformGrid
A UniformGrid is a grid whose cells all have the same size. You don’t place the children; they fill the cells in order. Rows and Columns fix the number of rows or columns; the other number follows from the number of children.






TipLab 2.8: UniformGrid



🎯 Goal. Six buttons of equal size in two rows.

Create UniformGridWindow (title UniformGrid, 360 × 320) and its launcher button.
Replace the window’s text with:
<UniformGrid Margin="16" Rows="2">
    <Button HorizontalAlignment="Stretch" VerticalAlignment="Stretch"
            HorizontalContentAlignment="Center" VerticalContentAlignment="Center">Button1</Button>
</UniformGrid>
Add Button2 to Button6 the same way.

✅ Check. Two rows of three buttons, all of the same size, filling the window.
💡 Try it. Replace Rows="2" by Columns="2", then remove one button.

title: 2  Layouts and Controls
text:
2.8 GridSplitter
A GridSplitter is a bar in a Grid that the user can drag to change the width of columns (or the height of rows) at runtime. Two properties matter:

ResizeDirection: always set it explicitly, to Columns or Rows.
HorizontalAlignment (for columns) decides which columns change: Left changes the splitter’s column and the one before it, Right its column and the one after it, and Stretch (the default) the columns on both sides of it. A splitter in the first column therefore needs HorizontalAlignment="Right"; without it, it tries to resize a column before column 0, and dragging does nothing.

MinWidth/MaxWidth on a ColumnDefinition limit how far the user can drag.






TipLab 2.9: GridSplitter



🎯 Goal. A grid whose column width can be changed with the mouse.

Create GridSplitterWindow (title GridSplitter, 420 × 360) and its launcher button.
Replace the window’s text with a <Grid Margin="16"> of two rows and two columns. Put <Button Content="Button 1" Margin="10"/> into the top-left cell and Button 2 into the bottom-right cell.
Add the splitter at the end of the grid:
<GridSplitter Grid.Column="0" Grid.RowSpan="2" Width="9" Background="Gray"
              ResizeDirection="Columns" HorizontalAlignment="Right"/>

✅ Check. A gray bar runs down the right edge of the left column. Dragging it makes the left column wider or narrower.
💡 Try it. Remove HorizontalAlignment="Right" and drag again. Then add MinWidth="80" to the first column definition (you need the long form of the definitions for that).

title: 2  Layouts and Controls
text:
2.9 ScrollViewer
Panels never scroll. If the content can be larger than the space available, wrap it in a ScrollViewer. It shows a vertical scrollbar when needed; the horizontal one is off unless you set HorizontalScrollBarVisibility (Auto shows it when needed, Visible always).
Two ways to break a line in a text:

in an attribute value, the XML character reference 
: Text="a
b",
inside a TextBlock’s content, the element <LineBreak/>.

One more thing about panels: a panel only receives mouse events where it has a background. If a panel should react to clicks but not be colored, set Background="Transparent".






TipLab 2.10: ScrollViewer



🎯 Goal. Content that is wider than the window, with a scrollbar.

Create ScrollViewerWindow (title ScrollViewer, 420 × 340) and its launcher button.
Replace the window’s text with:
<ScrollViewer Margin="16" HorizontalScrollBarVisibility="Visible">
    <Grid MinWidth="600" ColumnDefinitions="*,*">
    </Grid>
</ScrollViewer>
In the grid’s first column, add a TextBox with Margin="10" and the text a and b on two lines. In the second column, add a TextBlock with Margin="10" whose content is a b c d e f g, a <LineBreak/>, and h i.

✅ Check. A horizontal scrollbar is shown below the content. Scroll right to see the second column.
💡 Try it. Set HorizontalScrollBarVisibility="Auto" and make the window wider than 600 pixels.

title: 2  Layouts and Controls
2  Layouts and Controls
text:
2.11 Try it yourself

Build a login form with a Grid: two rows with a label and an input field each, labels in an Auto column, fields in a * column, and a right-aligned Login button below.
Rebuild the DockPanel window with a Grid. Which layout needs less XAML?
The launcher of LayoutDemo is too long for a small window. Make it scroll.

title: 3  Styles
text:
3.1 Styles and selectors
Setting FontSize="20" on every button of an app is tedious and error-prone. A style sets properties in one place, for all controls it applies to. Avalonia styles work much like CSS: a selector picks the controls, setters set their properties.
In the labs you build StylesDemo: one window with a tab per topic.
A style is a Style element with a Selector and one or more Setters:
The selector Button matches every button in the style’s scope. To style only some buttons, give them a style class and add it to the selector with a dot:
An element can have several classes (Classes="bigText danger"), and code can add and remove them at runtime (myButton.Classes.Add("bigText")). The selector always needs a type in front of the class (Button.bigText, not .bigText), so that the compiler knows which FontSize the setter means.
Other useful selector parts:

title: 3  Styles
3  Styles
3  Styles
text:
3.3 Pseudo-classes
Controls change their look in certain states: a button is hovered or pressed, a text box has the keyboard focus. Selectors react to such states with pseudo-classes, written with a colon:



Pseudo-class
The control …




:pointerover
is under the mouse pointer


:pressed
is being pressed


:focus
has the keyboard focus


:disabled
has IsEnabled="False"


:checked
is checked (CheckBox, ToggleButton, …)



<Style Selector="Button:pointerover">
    <Setter Property="FontWeight" Value="Bold"/>
</Style>
The style applies while the state lasts, and its setters are undone automatically when the state ends. Conditions are combined by writing them one after the other, without spaces: Button.save:pointerover matches only a button with the class save that is hovered.

title: 3  Styles
3  Styles
text:
3.5 Classes from data
A style class can be switched on and off by a binding. The syntax is Classes.<name>, bound to a bool:
<CheckBox Name="WarningCheck" Content="Show as warning"/>
<TextBlock Classes.warning="{Binding #WarningCheck.IsChecked}" Text="Disk almost full"/>
While the check box is checked, the TextBlock has the class warning, and a style TextBlock.warning applies. This is how a style reacts to data: the chapter Data Binding uses the same pattern to highlight list entries, bound to a property of the data instead of a check box.






TipLab 3.5: Classes from data



🎯 Goal. A check box that turns a message red.

Add a fifth tab Binding, built like the others.
Add the CheckBox and the TextBlock from the section above.
Write the style TextBlock.warning yourself: Foreground Red, FontWeight Bold.

✅ Check. Checking the box turns the text red and bold; unchecking it turns it back.

title: 3  Styles
3  Styles
3  Styles
text:
3.8 Try it yourself

Give all buttons of the States tab a Transitions block, so that their Opacity changes smoothly, and a :pointerover style that sets Opacity to 0.7.
Move the two caption styles from the Cascading tab into a file Styles/Captions.axaml and include it in App.axaml with StyleInclude.
Write a control template for a CheckBox that shows ON or OFF instead of a check mark. Hint: the pseudo-class :checked works in /template/ selectors, too.

title: 4  Data Binding and MVVM
text:
4.1 Data binding
In HelloAvalonia, every change of the state needed a line like CounterText.Text = "Counter: " + _counter;. Forget it once, and the screen shows old data. Data binding connects a control property to a data property, and keeps the two in sync automatically. On top of it sits the MVVM pattern, which this course uses from now on.
The labs have two parts. In the first, you rebuild HelloAvalonia with MVVM as HelloMvvm. In the second, you build DatabindingDemo, a list of people with a detail form.
A binding connects a target, a property of a control, with a source, a property of some object. The target must be a styled property (chapter Avalonia Basics); every property of the built-in controls that you would want to bind is one.
You have met bindings already, with another element as the source:

title: 4  Data Binding and MVVM
text:
<TextBox Name="TBRight"/>
<TextBox Text="{Binding #TBRight.Text}"/>

4.1.1 Binding modes







Mode
Direction




OneWay
source → target: the control shows the value


TwoWay
source ↔︎ target: the control shows the value, and user input changes it


OneTime
source → target, once, when the binding is created


OneWayToSource
target → source only



You rarely set a mode yourself. Properties that users edit (TextBox.Text, CheckBox.IsChecked, Slider.Value, ListBox.SelectedItem, …) default to TwoWay, all others to OneWay. User input is written to the source immediately, on every keystroke.

title: 4  Data Binding and MVVM
4  Data Binding and MVVM
4  Data Binding and MVVM
text:
4.4 Two-way binding
Input controls bind TwoWay by default, so the user can change any view model property directly: the text of a TextBox, the value of a Slider, the state of a CheckBox. The same property can be bound to several controls at once, and they all stay in sync.
A bool property can also switch a style class, as in the chapter Styles:
<TextBlock Text="{Binding Greeting}" Classes.bold="{Binding IsGreetingBold}"/>






TipLab 4.3: Two-way binding



🎯 Goal. A slider sets the size of the greeting, a check box makes it bold.

In the view model, add:
[ObservableProperty]
private double _greetingFontSize = 24;
In MainWindow.axaml, bind the greeting’s font size with FontSize="{Binding GreetingFontSize}" (instead of 24), and add below it:
<Slider Minimum="16" Maximum="48" Value="{Binding GreetingFontSize}"/>
On your own: add a bool property IsGreetingBold, a CheckBox Bold bound to it, and bind the class bold of the greeting to it. Define the style TextBlock.bold in <Window.Styles>.

✅ Check. Dragging the slider resizes the greeting, the check box switches bold on and off. There is still no event handler in your code.

HelloMvvm: add a Shout check box that shows the greeting in capital letters.
HelloMvvm: add a -5 button using the same IncrementByCommand.
DatabindingDemo: add an Add person button that adds a new, empty person to People and selects it, and a Remove button for the selected person.
DatabindingDemo: replace the detail form with a ContentControl and a keyed DataTemplate, as shown in the section Data templates. What happens to the form when nothing is selected?
